entries.h: 160 m / 80 m / 40 m power discrepancy - specific analysis
entries.x: Tablo-25, TAD v1.0 (BTK-official, dated one month after the Teknik Olcutler took effect), and the TRAC Adana mirror ALL THREE independently agree: 160 m = 9 W/30 W PEP; 80/40 m = 75 W/75 W. No evidence was found (mevzuat.gov.tr, resmigazete.gov.tr, btk.gov.tr searches) of a Board decision or amendment 2018-2026 raising these to 100 W/400 W. The Wikimedia (2022) document is a self-described compilation by a named individual (TA1HYK), not an official BTK publication, carries no document/version reference beyond "(2022)", and its 160/80/40 m figures do not match any of the three agreeing sources. Most plausible explanation: compiler transcription error (e.g. mixing the 20-m-and-above PEP column into the 160/80/40 m rows), not a genuine regulatory change. Conclusion : 9 W/30 W (160 m) and 75 W/75 W (80 m, 40 m) are the CURRENT LEGAL values. Wikimedia's 100 W/400 W figures should be marked INCORRECT / excluded as a site source unless a primary citation is later found.

entries.x: 2200 metres is the lowest-frequency amateur band, below medium wave, and propagates mainly by ground wave throughout the day; at night, as the ionospheric D layer weakens, the sky-wave contribution increases and the range widens. This band is suited to long-distance (DX) contacts using weak-signal techniques that require very narrow bandwidth, but daily variability is high and atmospheric noise (especially in the summer months) can make reception difficult.

The band uses almost exclusively CW and QRSS (very slow telegraphy) and narrowband digital modes; voice (phone) modes are impractical, because both transmitter power and antenna efficiency are low at these frequencies. Amateurs usually work with small loops or shortened antennas, and weak-signal digital modes (WSPR-like techniques) are common.
No separate centre of activity (spot) frequency is defined for this band.

The band is allocated to class A amateurs in Turkey; other classes cannot operate in this band. The TR table gives an output power limit for this band and the emission types are listed separately; for details see the TR legal table section of the page.

entries.h: What can be done on this band?

entries.x: 160 metres ("Top Band") is a classic night-time band: during the day, D-layer absorption largely extinguishes signals and range stays local or regional; at night, once the D layer disappears, intercontinental distances can open through F-layer reflections. Winter months and periods of low solar noise generally give better DX conditions; atmospheric noise (especially during summer thunderstorm periods) is a significant limiting factor.

The lower part of the band is reserved for CW and narrowband digital modes; SSB (phone) can be used in a specific part of the band and is mostly active at night. Large loops or shortened verticals are common because the length needed for a full-size dipole is impractical for most amateur sites.
1836 kHz is a centre of activity used as the gathering point for stations working CW QRP (low power).

The band is allocated to class A amateurs in Turkey. The TR table states that J3E (SSB) emission may be used only in the range 1832-1835 kHz; this restriction differs from the wider phone sub-band in the IARU Region 1 band plan, so care must be taken to stay within this narrow range when operating SSB from Turkey.

entries.h: What can be done on this band?

entries.x: 80 metres is a strong band for regional and intercontinental contacts at night; during the day, D-layer absorption limits range to the regional level (NVIS - near vertical incidence skywave - can be used for local/regional communication). Winter nights typically offer the best DX conditions; atmospheric noise rises in the summer months.

The lower part of the band is reserved for CW, the middle part for narrowband digital modes, and the remainder for all modes including SSB. There are preferred sub-segments for CW and SSB contests; the lowest and highest ends of the band are considered the priority for intercontinental work.

3555 kHz is the centre of activity for CW QRS (slow telegraphy) and 3560 kHz for CW QRP. 3630 kHz is the digital voice calling frequency, 3690 kHz is the SSB QRP centre of activity, and 3735 kHz is the centre of activity for image modes (such as SSTV/fax).
The band is allocated to class A amateurs in Turkey; the TR table contains a wide emission list (including CW and various digital and phone modes). International DX use of the band is widespread.

entries.h: What can be done on this band?

entries.x: 40 metres is a classic night/transition band, varying considerably across the day-night transition and suited to both local/regional and intercontinental contacts. During the day regional contacts generally dominate; at night, when the D layer disappears, range increases significantly and intercontinental DX conditions can develop. Strong broadcast stations in the 41 metre shortwave broadcast band directly above this band can cause interference at frequencies near the upper edge of the band, especially in the evening and at night.

The lower part of the band is reserved for CW, the middle part for narrowband digital modes (including common digital modes such as FT8/FT4), and the upper part for all modes including SSB. The upper part of the band is preferred for SSB contests; the topmost segment is considered the priority for intercontinental work.
7030 kHz is the centre of activity for CW QRP (low power) and 7090 kHz for SSB QRP. 7070 kHz is the digital voice calling frequency, and 7165 kHz is the centre of activity for image modes.

The band is open to class A and B amateurs in Turkey. For training and encouragement purposes, class B licence holders may operate in the lower part of the band (in the range 7000-7100 kHz) only with home-built equipment of at most 5 W output power; there is no such sub-range or power limit for class A.

entries.x: 20 metres is regarded as the busiest DX band in amateur radio; thanks to F-layer reflections, intercontinental contacts are often possible during daylight hours, and the band can stay open almost around the clock when the sunspot cycle is rising. The remainder of the band is open to all modes including SSB; there is also an area where DXpeditions have priority.

entries.h: What can be done on this band?

entries.x: 10 metres is the HF band most sensitive to solar activity: during high-sunspot periods worldwide DX openings can occur through F-layer reflections, while during low-activity periods the band can stay closed for days. The band contains CW, narrowband digital modes, various beacon segments, general-purpose all-mode sections, FM simplex and repeater channels, and a section reserved for amateur-satellite links; this gives 10 metres the most varied usage profile among the HF bands. FM repeater inputs and outputs are in separate sub-segments (the RH1-RH8 channel system).

28055 kHz (QRS) and 28060 kHz (QRP) are centres of activity (CW). 28330 kHz is the digital voice calling frequency, 28360 kHz is the SSB QRP centre of activity, and 28680 kHz is the centre of activity for image modes. 29600 kHz is the FM calling channel and 29610 kHz is the FM simplex repeater (parrot, with input and output on the same frequency) channel.

The band is open to class A and B amateurs in Turkey; class B licence holders may operate in the whole band with home-built equipment of at most 5 W output power. F3E/G3E (wideband FM) cannot be used in the range 28000-29500 kHz; beacons may operate at up to 25 W in the range 28-28.5 MHz.

entries.h: What can be done on this band?

entries.x: 6 metres is known as the "magic band"; most of the time it is limited to normal tropospheric range, but during periods when Sporadic-E layers form (especially in the summer months) sudden and strong openings reaching very long distances can occur. During periods of high solar cycle activity, longer-distance DX openings through F2-layer reflections may also be possible; in addition, communication by non-ionospheric paths, using meteor scatter and Earth-Moon-Earth (EME) techniques, is also practised on this band.

The lower part of the band is reserved for CW (including the Synchronized Beacon Project), the middle part for SSB/CW, and the upper parts for narrowband digital modes, EME and meteor scatter activity. The all-mode segments also contain FM simplex, digital voice internet gateways and FM/DV repeater channels; the upper end of the band is for all-mode use, divided into blocks according to national planning.

50050 kHz is the future international centre of activity for CW and 50090 kHz is the CW intercontinental centre of activity. 50110 kHz is a centre of activity used only for the intercontinental calling, and 50150 kHz is the international centre of activity. 50305 kHz is the PSK centre of activity, 50630 kHz is the digital voice calling frequency, and 51510 kHz is the FM calling channel.

The band is open to class A and B amateurs in Turkey; the TR allocation is limited to 50-52 MHz (the IARU Region 1 plan extends up to 54 MHz, but the range 52-54 MHz has no legal counterpart in Turkey). Earth-Moon-Earth (EME) communication can also be carried out on this band; the maximum output power of beacons is 25 W.

entries.x: The 70 MHz (4 metre) band is NOT allocated to the amateur radio service in the current BTK 2022 amateur table. Therefore amateurs in Turkey cannot legally transmit in this band. The information below is given for general context only, based on the IARU Region 1 band plan.

4 metres has a propagation character between 6 metres and 2 metres; under normal conditions it is limited to tropospheric range, while medium-to-long distance contacts may be possible during Sporadic-E openings. entries.h: What can be done on this band?

entries.x: 2 metres is a VHF band limited mainly to line-of-sight and tropospheric range. Under tropospheric ducting conditions the range can increase significantly; during the Sporadic-E season very long-distance openings can occasionally be seen. Meteor scatter and Earth-Moon-Earth (EME) techniques are also used on this band for weak-signal DX work.

The lower end of the band has satellite downlinks (downlink only), followed by CW and weak-signal MGM/EME segments, the middle part for SSB/CW/MGM, and the upper part for FM/digital voice repeater input and output channels, space communication, and finally a section reserved for satellite use only. Image modes (SSTV/Fax), APRS and digital voice internet gateways are also in the all-mode segment.

144050 kHz is the CW centre of activity and 144300 kHz is the SSB centre of activity. 144500 kHz is the centre of activity for image modes (SSTV/Fax), 144800 kHz is the frequency used for APRS, and 145500 kHz is the FM calling channel (channel designator V40).

The band is open to class A, B and C amateurs in Turkey; class C licence holders may operate with at most 5 W output power. The band is also used for the amateur-satellite service; the maximum transmitter output power for handheld radios in FM mode is 5 W. Earth-Moon-Earth (EME) communication is permitted; the maximum output power of repeater equipment installed by amateur radio associations is 25 W, and the maximum equipment output power of beacons is 25 W.

entries.h: What can be done on this band?

entries.x: 70 centimetres, like 2 metres, is a UHF band largely limited to line-of-sight; reflection/diffraction effects from buildings and obstacles are more pronounced than on 2 metres, which makes urban repeater use valuable. Under tropospheric ducting conditions the range can extend significantly; Earth-Moon-Earth (EME) techniques are also used on this band for weak-signal DX work.

The band contains input/output channel blocks reserved for different regional repeater systems (such as the F/PA/ON system and the Region 1 system, with different frequency shifts), an all-mode segment for CW/SSB/telegraphy, a beacon segment, a wide section for the satellite service and digital ATV (amateur television), and also FM/digital voice simplex channels.
432200 kHz is the SSB centre of activity, 433500 kHz is the FM calling channel (channel designator U280), and 437000 kHz is the digital ATV/data centre of activity.

The band is open to class A, B and C amateurs in Turkey; class C licence holders may operate with at most 5 W output power. The TR allocation is not a single range but the union of several separate sub-bands (430.200-430.700, 431.550-431.825, 432.000-432.975, 433.400-433.575, 435.000-437.975 and 439.150-439.425 MHz); the sub-bands 431.550-431.825 and 439.150-439.425 MHz are reserved for repeater equipment installed by amateur radio associations. The 432 MHz region is also used for amateur-satellite and EME communication; the maximum transmitter output power for handheld radios in FM mode is 5 W, and the maximum equipment output power of beacons is 25 W.

entries.h: What can be done on this band?

entries.x: 23 centimetres is a UHF band limited entirely to line-of-sight; techniques such as rain scatter and tropospheric ducting can extend the range. Earth-Moon-Earth (EME) communication is a weak-signal technique especially favoured on this band because of its advantages of higher antenna gain and lower atmospheric noise.

The lower part of the band is reserved for future use; after it come digital communication and repeater output channel blocks. The satellite service is in the middle part; in the upper section there are repeater input channels, followed by narrowband and wideband centres of activity for CW/SSB/MGM, linear transponder inputs/outputs, image modes, experimental MGM and a local beacon segment. At the very top there are FM and digital voice simplex channels.
1296200 kHz is the narrowband centre of activity and 1297500 kHz is the FM centre of activity.

The band is open to class A and B amateurs in Turkey; the maximum output power in handheld FM mode is 5 W and EME is permitted. entries.h: Two different sources, two different meanings
entries.x: The charts and tables on every band page show two independent data layers on top of each other (overlay); they do not merge them: Turkey (BTK 2022): legal allocation status - BTK Technical Criteria decision no. 2022/IK-SYD/245, ARTICLE 22. [1] This layer shows what is legally permitted in Turkey. IARU Region 1: voluntary usage recommendation - the IARU Region 1 HF Band Plan (as of 16 October 2020) [2] and, for 50 MHz and above, the IARU Region 1 VHF Handbook, version 10.03. [3] This layer is a mode/usage recommendation; it is not part of TR legislation. Where the Handbook and the older one-page summary plans conflict at 50 MHz and above, the Handbook is taken as authoritative. [3] Differences between the two layers (e.g. a band that is not allocated in Turkey but appears in the IARU plan, or a use that TR permits but the IARU plan does not recommend) are deliberately not hidden ; they are shown on separate rows in the chart.

In the spectrum chart on each band page, the upper row shows the Turkey legal status (green: allocated, hatched pattern: not allocated; in the lower sub-row, class A/B/C access bars), and the lower row shows the IARU Region 1 usage segments (coloured by mode). Triangle markers show specific (spot) frequencies. Because the chart is only a visual summary, tables containing the same data are placed below the chart (for keyboard and screen reader access). Colour coding alone does not carry meaning: every segment also has a text label/tooltip, and the palette has been chosen to be suitable for colour-blind users.

Allocated in TR / Not allocated in TR - shows whether a band is allocated to the amateur service in Turkey's 2022 table. Verified / Secondary source / Unverified - shows how directly/clearly the value is printed in the source document: Verified: the value is printed directly and clearly in the source document. Secondary source: the value was taken from a reliable secondary source (e.g. a news/report summary) rather than from the primary source itself. Unverified: the source cell is merged, illegible or missing; the value has not been guessed and is explicitly marked "unverified".

entries.h: Frequency units and whole-number Hz representation
entries.x: In the data layer of the site every frequency is stored as an integer in Hz (e.g. 144.000 MHz = 144000000 Hz); this avoids rounding/binary-fraction errors in kHz/MHz/GHz displays. On screen the value is converted to the unit appropriate to the band group (kHz for LF/MF, MHz for VHF/UHF, GHz for SHF/EHF) and shown with an explicit unit label; the unit is never changed silently.

Symbol Meaning Example values occurring on this site 1st symbol (letter) Type of modulation of the main carrier A: double-sideband AM, F: FM, G: phase modulation, H: full-carrier SSB, J: suppressed-carrier SSB, R: reduced/variable-level carrier SSB 2nd symbol (digit) Nature of the modulating signal 1: single channel of digital information without a subcarrier (e.g. keyed CW), 2: single channel of digital information with a subcarrier, 3: single channel of analogue information (e.g. voice) 3rd symbol (letter) Type of information transmitted A: telegraphy for aural reception (Morse/CW), B: telegraphy for automatic reception, C: facsimile, D: data/telemetry, E: telephony (voice), F: television/video Example: A1A = double-sideband AM carrier (A), digital without subcarrier (1), telegraphy for aural reception (A) - that is, keyed Morse/CW. J3E = suppressed-carrier SSB (J), single-channel analogue (3), telephony/voice (E).

Short explanations of general radio terms used on the site. This glossary explains general radio/engineering terms used on the site; the definitions below are general technical knowledge and are not attributed to a particular regulatory document. For this site's own terms such as class, allocation and confidence level, links to the relevant pages are given.
A frequency range with specific lower and upper frequency limits reserved for the amateur radio service (e.g. the 2 metre band: 144-146 MHz).
A narrower sub-range within a band that is recommended or allocated for a specific use/mode (e.g. the CW segment of a band).
The official assignment of a frequency range by the relevant regulator to a particular radio service (e.g. the amateur service).

A short code describing the modulation/information-carrying form of the signal produced by a transmitter (e.g. A1A: keyed telegraphy/CW for aural reception). Detailed explanation: emission designators page .
One of the three grades in which an amateur radio licence is issued in Turkey; each class has different band/power access. Details: licence classes page .
A fixed station that receives a signal on one frequency and retransmits it on another frequency, usually to cover a wider area.
A direct station-to-station mode of operation in which transmitter and receiver use the same frequency (no repeater is used).
An operating mode in which communication between two ground stations is achieved by reflecting the signal off the surface of the Moon (moonbounce).
The service category reserved for communication between amateur radio stations via amateur satellites in orbit.
The power value at the highest point of a transmitter's modulation envelope; a different measure from average output power.
The effective power an antenna system radiates in a given direction relative to an ideal (isotropic) antenna; a combined measure of transmitter output power and antenna gain.
A single frequency point within a band that is commonly used for a specific purpose (e.g. a calling channel, a centre of activity).
A channel numbering system used on VHF/UHF FM bands, generated from a specific base frequency and step interval (e.g. V40, U280).

entries.h: Threat to the 70 cm band: AST SpaceMobile TT&C use
entries.x: Verified According to the October 2025 meeting summary of the IARU Administrative Council, AST & Science LLC (AST SpaceMobile) wants to use the 430-440 MHz amateur and amateur-satellite band for telemetry, tracking and command (TT&C) purposes for its system that aims to provide voice communication directly to handheld devices via low-Earth-orbit satellites. The FCC Space Bureau granted the company a licence for this band on 29 August 2025; however, the licence covers only 20 additional satellites instead of the 243 requested and limits use to the launch and early orbit phase (LEOP) and to unusual satellite operating situations, for a period of at most 24 hours. The IARU considers the use of ITU Radio Regulations Article 4.4 on this matter inappropriate. How this site is generated and published, and what is not published.

This site is generated automatically from the band data (YAML) and the research documents in the private repository ta1rjv/Turkiye-HAMBandPlan. Every number on the band pages is read from the same data files; it is never copied by hand into Markdown pages. The spectrum charts are static SVG images drawn from the same data.

A GitHub Actions workflow in the repository does the work. The unit tests run first, then the site is built and passes a leak gate (secrets, private network addresses, local file paths, e-mail addresses) before it may be published. The result is pushed to the public repository of this site (ta1rjv/bandplan) and served with GitHub Pages. Only the generated site is in the public repository; the source data repository is private.
Project status and planning files, raw source documents (PDF files, text dumps) and tool-specific configuration are not published. The sources page gives the official online link of every source.

The charts are static; there is no zoom and no class filter. Class access is given as a list on every band page. Part of the English text has not been translated yet; those pages show the Turkish text. The research documents are English only.
